title: Journey 3: Cloud Run L4 GPU & Vertex AI Inference Architecture
description: Master the TTFT/cost crossover between Gemma 4 on Cloud Run L4 GPUs and Vertex AI Gemini 3.8 Flash, continuous batching concurrency in Terraform, and automated post-evaluation GCS/BigQuery resource teardown.

nodes.title: Node 1: Warm L4 GPU VRAM vs. Scale-to-Zero Cold Starts & CPU Memory Bandwidth
nodes.objective: Understand why open-weight Gemma 4 inference requires dedicated L4 GPU memory bandwidth with min_instance_count >= 1 for interactive latency, and when serverless Vertex AI Gemini 3.8 Flash is more cost-effective.

primaryModality.questionPrompt:
### Node 1: Cloud Run L4 GPU vs. CPU & Vertex AI Crossover
Drag the **Daily Requests** and **Min Warm Instances** sliders below to inspect the impact on Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and daily cost:

{{WIDGET_EMBED}}

You are deploying a **Gemma 4** microservice on Cloud Run (`nvidia-l4`, 24 GB VRAM) for an interactive agent studio requiring **<250ms p95 TTFT** under sustained traffic (80k requests/day). What happens if you set `min_instance_count = 0` or drop the GPU to run on CPU-only Cloud Run instances?
options: Option A — Setting `min_instance_count = 0` triggers multi-gigabyte model weight loading into GPU VRAM on idle wakeups (~14s+ cold-start spike), while CPU-only instances lack the memory bandwidth for autoregressive decoding (~4,200ms+ TTFT); keeping `min_instance_count = 1` with `cpu_idle = false` preserves warm VRAM at ~185ms TTFT.

Option B — Cloud Run automatically snapshots GPU VRAM across scale-to-zero transitions with zero cold-start latency, and CPU-only instances match L4 token throughput as long as vCPU count is set to 8.
Option C — Running Gemma 4 weights directly on the developer's local Apple Silicon MacBook via unrolled Python loops is the recommended production fallback when Cloud Run scales to zero.

1.diagnosis: Autoregressive LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: an NVIDIA L4 GPU provides ~300 GB/s of VRAM bandwidth, whereas standard Cloud Run CPU memory bandwidth bottlenecks token generation to >4 seconds TTFT. Furthermore, scaling a GPU container to zero (`min_instance_count = 0`) evicts model weights from VRAM, causing a 10–15+ second cold start on the next request.

2.diagnosis: Heavy weight loading or unrolled autoregressive loops on a local Apple Silicon host risk triggering macOS kernel memory watchdog panics. Production and heavy evaluation workloads belong on Cloud Run L4 GPUs or Vertex AI.

remediationModality.questionPrompt:
### Node 1 (Remediation View): Terraform Diff & Cold-Start Sequence
Let's switch from the simulator to the exact **Terraform configuration diff (`cloud_run_l4_service.tf`)** and request latency trace:

```diff
@@ -14,10 +14,11 @@ resource "google_cloud_run_v2_service" "gemma4_l4" {
   template {
-    max_instance_request_concurrency = 1
+    max_instance_request_concurrency = 32
     scaling {
-      min_instance_count = 0
+      min_instance_count = 1
       max_instance_count = 4
     }
     containers {
       resources {
         limits = { cpu = "8", memory = "32Gi", "nvidia.com/gpu" = "1" }
-        cpu_idle = true
+        cpu_idle = false
       }
     }
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as Agent Studio
    participant Cold as L4 (min_instance=0)
    participant Warm as L4 (min_instance=1, concurrency=32)
    Client->>Cold: POST /v1/chat/completions
    Note over Cold: Pull container + load 16GB weights into VRAM (~14.8s)
    Cold-->>Client: First token after 14,800ms
    Client->>Warm: POST /v1/chat/completions
    Note over Warm: Weights already resident in L4 VRAM + PagedAttention
    Warm-->>Client: First token after 185ms
```

Looking at the Terraform diff and sequence trace above, why must `min_instance_count = 1`, `cpu_idle = false`, and `max_instance_request_concurrency = 32` be configured together on the Cloud Run L4 service?
options: Option A — `min_instance_count = 1` and `cpu_idle = false` keep the Gemma 4 weights resident in L4 VRAM with active background health/scheduler threads, while `max_instance_request_concurrency = 32` allows vLLM continuous batching to serve 32 concurrent streams on a single GPU instead of spinning up 32 separate GPUs.
Option B — Setting `max_instance_request_concurrency = 1` is required because an NVIDIA L4 GPU can only hold one HTTP connection in VRAM at a time.
Option C — `cpu_idle = true` throttles the CPU between tokens to make GPU matrix multiplication run faster.

1.diagnosis: If `max_instance_request_concurrency = 1`, 32 concurrent requests would force Cloud Run to attempt provisioning 32 separate L4 GPU instances (exhausting regional GPU quota). vLLM continuous batching shares a single L4 GPU across 32 concurrent requests.

2.diagnosis: Cloud Run GPU containers require `cpu_idle = false` (always-allocated CPU) so the inference server's async event loop and CUDA kernel scheduler are never throttled.

nodes.title: Node 2: Automated Resource Lifecycle & Post-Evaluation Teardown
nodes.objective: Ensure every cloud benchmark or evaluation harness uses Application Default Credentials (ADC) and guarantees post-run teardown of temporary GCS staging objects and BigQuery tables inside a try/finally block.

primaryModality.questionPrompt:
### Node 2: Cloud Benchmark Resource Lifecycle & Auth Hygiene
Compare these two Python benchmark harnesses that evaluate Gemma 4 latency and stage telemetry to Cloud Storage (`gs://davenport-boutique-vertex-staging/`) and BigQuery (`davenport-boutique`):
options:
Option A — ADC Auth + Guaranteed `try / finally` Resource Teardown:
```python
def run_ephemeral_l4_eval(run_id: str, client: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    gcs_prefix = f"gs://davenport-boutique-vertex-staging/eval-{run_id}"
    bq_table = f"davenport-boutique.eval_scratch.l4_metrics_{run_id}"
    try:
        client.stage_prompts(gcs_prefix)
        return client.execute_benchmark(gcs_prefix, bq_table)
    finally:
        # Always clean up ephemeral cloud artifacts even if the benchmark raises!
        client.delete_gcs_prefix(gcs_prefix)
        client.drop_bigquery_table(bq_table)
```

Option B — Hardcoded API Key + Teardown Only on Happy Path:
```python
def run_ephemeral_l4_eval(run_id: str, client: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    api_key = os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"]  # Fails under ADC-only project policy
    gcs_prefix = f"gs://davenport-boutique-vertex-staging/eval-{run_id}"
    bq_table = f"davenport-boutique.eval_scratch.l4_metrics_{run_id}"
    result = client.execute_benchmark(gcs_prefix, bq_table, api_key=api_key)
    client.delete_gcs_prefix(gcs_prefix)
    return result
```

1.diagnosis: Option B violates two core engineering rules: it checks for `GEMINI_API_KEY` instead of using Google Cloud Application Default Credentials (ADC), and because cleanup is outside a `finally` block, any benchmark exception leaves orphaned GCS objects and BigQuery scratch tables accumulating storage charges.

2.diagnosis: Option C violates the Strict Never Mock Directive: catching a real service error and returning synthetic benchmark metrics (`simulated_success`) hides broken infrastructure and corrupts evaluation results.

remediationModality.questionPrompt:
### Node 2 (Remediation View): Exception-Safe Teardown Diff
Examine why placing cloud cleanup calls inside a `finally:` block is mandatory for any evaluation harness:

```diff
@@ -8,6 +8,8 @@ def run_ephemeral_l4_eval(run_id: str, client: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
-    client.stage_prompts(gcs_prefix)
-    result = client.execute_benchmark(gcs_prefix, bq_table)
-    client.delete_gcs_prefix(gcs_prefix)
-    client.drop_bigquery_table(bq_table)
-    return result
+    try:
+        client.stage_prompts(gcs_prefix)
+        return client.execute_benchmark(gcs_prefix, bq_table)
+    finally:
+        client.delete_gcs_prefix(gcs_prefix)
+        client.drop_bigquery_table(bq_table)
```

If `client.execute_benchmark()` raises a `TimeoutError` halfway through the run, what is the difference between the `-` (before) code and the `+` (after) code?
options: Option A — In the `+` (after) code, Python executes the `finally:` block before propagating the `TimeoutError`, guaranteeing that both `delete_gcs_prefix` and `drop_bigquery_table` run and zero orphaned cloud resources remain.
Option B — The `finally:` block swallows the `TimeoutError` and returns `None` so the test appears to pass.
Option C — The `finally:` block only runs when `execute_benchmark()` succeeds without throwing an exception.

1.diagnosis: A `try / finally` block in Python does NOT swallow exceptions (unless `finally` itself executes a `return` or `break`). It runs the cleanup actions and then re-raises the original `TimeoutError`.

2.diagnosis: In Python, `finally:` always executes whether the `try:` block returns normally or raises an exception.
